one_liner: This book provides a comprehensive, unified treatment of Kolmogorov complexity and algorithmic randomness, linking information theory, computability, and probability to formalize the notion of randomness in individual strings.
paragraphs: The book addresses the fundamental question of how to measure the information content or randomness of a single string, rather than relying on statistical properties of ensembles. Traditional probability theory struggles to define randomness for individual objects, so Kolmogorov complexity offers a solution by defining the complexity of a string as the length of the shortest program that can generate it. This approach shifts the focus from average-case analysis to individual object analysis, enabling a rigorous foundation for algorithmic randomness that bridges computer science and mathematical logic.

The authors systematically develop multiple variants of Kolmogorov complexity—plain, prefix, and monotone—and connect them to semimeasures, martingales, and effective null sets. They use algorithmic methods from computability theory to define randomness via unpredictability (Martin-Löf tests), incompressibility, and the failure of computable betting strategies. The book also introduces conditional complexity, information distance, and connections to Shannon entropy, creating a unified framework that compares different notions of randomness and complexity through formal inequalities and combinatorial interpretations.

Key results include the equivalence between Martin-Löf randomness, incompressibility, and unpredictability via martingales; the Levin-Schnorr theorem linking prefix complexity to randomness; and applications ranging from number theory (infinitely many primes) to computational limits of finite automata. The practical implications extend to data compression, cryptography, machine learning (model selection via minimum description length), and the foundations of statistics—where Kolmogorov complexity provides a formal basis for Occam’s razor. The book also explores deep connections between information theory and logic, showing how complexity can characterize logical provability and inference.
key_takeaways: Kolmogorov complexity measures the randomness of an individual string by the length of its shortest generating program.
Algorithmic randomness can be defined in multiple equivalent ways: incompressibility, Martin-Löf tests, and failure of computable martingales.
Prefix complexity (with self-delimiting programs) is more robust than plain complexity and forms the basis for modern algorithmic information theory.
Kolmogorov complexity provides a theoretical foundation for Occam’s razor, linking simplicity to predictive power in data analysis and machine learning.
The book unifies information theory, computability, and probability through inequalities involving entropy, complexity, and common information.
eli5: Imagine you have a secret code that can draw a picture. If the code is super short, like 'draw a square', then the picture isn't very random. But if you need a super long code with lots of details to draw it, then the picture is random. This book teaches us how to measure how 'random' any drawing (or string of letters) is by finding the shortest code that can make it.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of computability theory and Turing machines
Familiarity with probability theory and information entropy
applications: Data compression algorithms that use algorithmic complexity to find the most efficient encoding
Cryptography and random number generation by testing for algorithmic randomness
title: Kolmogorov Complexity
